issues.legal_issue: A statutory reference to an existing civil court, rather than to its presiding officer as an individual, is a reference to the court and not to a persona designata.
material_facts: A Magistrate referred to a civil court the question of which party had possession of the disputed property at the relevant time.
The reference was to a constituted civil court, not to the presiding Judge of a particular court as an individual.
issues.conclusion: The reference was to a constituted court and not to a persona designata.
issues.legal_principle: A reference by a special or local law to a constituted court as a court, without naming its presiding officer, is not a reference to a persona designata. The Court applied the distinction between a persona designata and a legal tribunal explained in Balakrishna Udayar v. Vasudeva Aiyar and the meaning of persona designata accepted in Central Talkies Ltd. v. Dwarka Prasad.

predicates.magistrate_possession_reference: A Magistrate referred a dispute about possession to a civil court for determination.
predicates.special_law_names_existing_court: The governing law directed that the question be referred to an existing court as a court.
predicates.reference_does_not_name_presiding_office: The reference identified the court rather than its presiding officer as an individual.

issues.definition: When a Magistrate makes a possession reference under a law that identifies an existing court rather than its presiding officer, the reference is to the constituted court.

issues.legal_issue: A superior court may transfer to another competent subordinate court a judicial proceeding pending before a civil court on a Magistrate’s reference concerning possession.
material_facts: A Magistrate referred a possession question to a civil court, where the reference remained pending.
The District Judge transferred the reference from one subordinate civil court to another court competent to decide it.
The proceeding required judicial adjudication of the possession dispute.
issues.conclusion: The District Judge had jurisdiction to transfer the reference under the general transfer power in the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure covers an “other proceeding” pending in a subordinate court; the term is comprehensive and is not limited to civil proceedings. The ordinary rules of procedure applicable to courts generally apply to a proceeding before a civil court on a reference under section 146(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court relied on Adaikappa Chettiar v. Chandrasekhara Thevar, Maung Ba Thaw v. Ma Pin, South Asia Industries (P) Ltd. v. S. B. Sarup Singh, Narayan Row v. Ishwarlal, and Kochadai Naidu v. Nagavasami Naidu. The bar on appeal or revision from the civil court’s finding under section 146(1-D) of the Code of Criminal Procedure follows from that express provision, not from the proceeding being non-civil. The Court stated obiter that the proceeding is also a civil proceeding contemplated by section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but held that resort to section 141 was unnecessary to decide the transfer issue.

rule.if: magistrate_possession_reference_to_civil_court and reference_pending_in_subordinate_court and proceeding_requires_judicial_adjudication and transferee_court_competent

predicates.magistrate_possession_reference_to_civil: A Magistrate referred a possession dispute for determination by a civil court.
predicates.reference_pending_in_subordinate_court: The reference was pending before a court subordinate to the court exercising the transfer power.
predicates.proceeding_requires_judicial_adjudicatio: The matter before the civil court required judicial determination of a dispute.
predicates.transferee_court_competent: The court to which the matter was transferred was competent to determine it.

issues.definition: A superior court may transfer a Magistrate’s possession reference when it is pending before a subordinate court, requires judicial adjudication, and can be decided by the proposed transferee court.
